links.note: Four reasons asked; the answer develops (a) at length - hand printing in China, Japan and Korea, books printed from AD 594, and Marco Polo returning in 1295 with the knowledge. That is 23906, print reaching Europe through trade with China. Parts (b) and (c) reach 23909 and (d) 23921.

Three short notes; the answer develops the Gutenberg Press - the olive press as model, moulds for casting metal type, 26 Roman characters, perfected by 1448. 23907. Erasmus belongs to 23909 and the Vernacular Press Act to 23921.

Three groups asked; the answer opens on and develops (a) Women - women's lives and feelings written about, reading rising in middle-class homes, women's schools. That is 23919. (b) reaches 23920 and (c) 23917.

Marco Polo as the Italian traveller - he is in the chapter only as the carrier of woodblock printing knowledge from China to Europe, which is 23906. 23903 is the East Asian technology itself, before it travelled.

The Protestant Reformation aiming to reform the Catholic Church is the religious-debate passage where print carried Luther's challenge, 23909. NOTE: the second option is labelled '(ft)' instead of '(b)'.
Rammohun Roy publishing the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821 is the reform-and-public-debate passage in the India section, 23917. 23921 is the later censorship of the nationalist press, a different phase.

Asks what ancient Indian manuscripts were written on - 23914, India's manuscript tradition copied on palm leaf and handmade paper. DEFECT: the key is marked 'Vellum', which is European animal-skin parchment. The correct option is (c) palm leaves; the key is wrong.
The Reformation launched against the Catholic Church's corrupt practices - the same religious-dissent passage as qid:106243, 23909.

Jane Austen, the Bronte sisters and George Eliot are named in the nineteenth-century EUROPEAN passage on women as a new category of readers and writers, which is 23912. 23919 is the India-specific women-and-print section, and the odd-one-out here (Gorky) is European too.
Italians getting woodblock printing from China is 23906's description directly.

Aristocrats still buying luxury editions handwritten on expensive vellum while merchants and students bought cheap printed copies - the passage in which manuscripts could not meet Europe's demand, 23906. 23915 carries the same argument for INDIAN manuscripts, which this stem excludes by saying 'in Europe'.
Why handwritten manuscripts stayed limited in Europe - fragile, awkward, expensive to copy; the false option is that their content was seditious. 23906 holds the Europe case; 23915 is the Indian one.
Gutenberg in Germany as the inventor of the first known printing press - 23907.
